mainTopic: The dignity exemption in returning lost items, acting beyond the letter of the law, and when a found animal counts as lost
overview: The amud opens by finishing a source: your own loss comes before your friend's, learned from 'לא יהיה בך אביון'. So the word 'והתעלמת' must teach something else: a זקן does not have to return an item when handling it is beneath his dignity. רבה adds that once he starts handling the animal, he must finish, as the story of אביי and the goats shows. The גמרא leaves unresolved (תיקו) whether someone who would return an item in the field must also return it in the city. רבא gives a simple test: whatever you would do for your own property, you must do for your friend's. The story of רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי, who bought a man's wood rather than lift it, leads to a question about הפקר and to the idea of acting לפנים משורת הדין. That idea is backed by רב יוסף's ברייתא and by רבי יוחנן's teaching that ירושלים was destroyed because people never went beyond strict law. A new משנה then defines which animals count as lost, requires returning one again and again, and sets the finder's pay. The גמרא explains the משנה's wording and adds רב's three-day rule for animals seen grazing at dawn and dusk. A supporting ברייתא begins at the end of the amud and continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Your own loss comes first: the source verse
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes quoting the פסוק 'לא יהיה בך אביון' and learns from it that your own property comes before anyone else's.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'There shall be no needy among you' teaches that your own property comes before the property of any other person.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is completing an earlier point. The rule that your own loss comes before your friend's loss is learned from this פסוק, not from 'והתעלמת'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק is read as an instruction: make sure you yourself do not become needy. So when you must choose between saving your own item and returning someone else's, your own item comes first. Because this rule already has its own source, the extra word in the אבידה section is free to teach something else.

keyTerms.meaning: Before that of any other person

phrases.english: 'There shall be no needy among you'
phrases.notes: דברים 15:4. The quote starts on the previous amud.

phrases.english: yours comes before that of any other person.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the suggestion (begun on the previous amud) that 'והתעלמת' teaches that one's own loss comes first, since that rule is already learned from 'לא יהיה בך אביון'.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that a person's own loss takes priority over another person's loss.
steps.raayaSupportSource: דברים 15:4, 'אפס כי לא יהיה בך אביון'

steps.title: The verse teaches the exemption of an elderly person
steps.stepSummary: Since the 'own loss first' rule has its own source, the גמרא concludes that 'והתעלמת' teaches that a זקן is exempt when the task is beneath his dignity.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the verse is needed for an elderly person, when returning the item is not fitting for his dignity.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא settles what the word 'והתעלמת' comes to teach. It teaches the case of a זקן for whom handling the item would be undignified.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The other possible teachings are already covered by other sources. So the only thing left for this word to teach is that a respected elderly person may 'ignore' a lost item that would be humiliating for him to tend. This is an exception within the מצוה of השבת אבידה. The מצוה itself still stands.
steps.whatToRemember: A זקן does not have to return a lost item if handling it is beneath his dignity. This is learned from 'והתעלמת'.

phrases.english: Rather, it is needed for an elderly person
phrases.notes: 'It' means the word 'והתעלמת' that the גמרא has been trying to explain.

phrases.english: when it is not in keeping with his dignity.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion made possible by step 1.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The word 'והתעלמת' teaches the exemption of a זקן for whom returning the item is undignified.

steps.title: Once he strikes the animal, he is obligated
steps.stepSummary: רבה rules that if the exempt person strikes the animal even once to move it, he becomes obligated to return it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: If he struck it, he is obligated regarding it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה adds a limit to the זקן's exemption. If he starts dealing with the animal, he loses the exemption.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The exemption lets a זקן avoid getting involved. But once he acts, for example by hitting the animal to steer it, he has started the return. Now he must finish it.

keyTerms.meaning: He struck it (to drive it along)

phrases.english: Rabba said:
If he struck it, he is obligated regarding it.
phrases.notes: 'It' is a lost animal that the elderly person would normally be exempt from returning.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sets a limit on the זקן exemption established in step 2.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An exempt person who begins handling the animal (by striking it) becomes obligated to return it.

steps.title: אביי throws a clod at the goats
steps.stepSummary: אביי throws a clod of dirt at some goats, and רבה tells him he is now obligated to return them.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי was sitting before רבה and saw some goats standing there. He picked up a clod of earth and threw it at them. רבה said to him: You have become obligated for them. Get up and return them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story that shows רבה's rule in real life.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Throwing a clod made the goats move, so it counts like 'striking' them. Even this small act was enough for רבה to rule that אביי was now obligated to return them.
steps.confusionAlert: אביי was not doing anything wrong. He simply moved the goats, and by doing so he took on the duty to return them.

phrases.english: Abaye was sitting before Rabba,
he saw these goats that were standing there,
he took a clod of earth and threw it at them.
He said to him: You have become obligated for them,
phrases.notes: 'He' here is רבה, speaking to אביי.

phrases.english: get up and return them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Illustrates רבה's ruling from step 3 with an actual event.
steps.raayaObject: רבה's rule that starting to handle the animal creates an obligation.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבה's own ruling to אביי about the goats.

steps.title: Would return in the field but not in the city
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks about a person who would return this kind of item in the field but not in the city.
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked: If it is his way to return such an item in the field, but not in the city, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets up a new question. The next step lays out the two sides.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the field few people see him, so handling the item is not embarrassing. In the city it would be beneath his dignity. The question is what happens when the return starts in the field and must continue into the city.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was asked among them
It is his way to return

phrases.english: It was asked of them:
If it is his way to return it in the field,
but it is not his way to return it in the city, what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new question that builds on the זקן exemption and רבה's rule.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a person who would return the item in the field, but not in the city, is obligated.

steps.title: The two sides of the question
steps.stepSummary: Either a full השבה is required, so he is exempt, or his obligation in the field carries over into the city.
steps.simpleTranslation: Do we say that we need a complete return, and since it is not his way to return in the city, he should not be obligated? Or perhaps, he is at least obligated in the field, and since he is obligated there, he is obligated in the city too?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the two possible ways to look at the question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Side one: the obligation must be a complete return, all the way to the owner. Since he would not do the city part, he is not obligated at all. Side two: the obligation clearly starts in the field, and once it starts it continues all the way, even in the city.

phrases.english: Do we say that we need a complete return,
and since it is not his way to return in the city,
he should not be obligated?
Or perhaps, in the field at least
he is obligated for it,
and since he is obligated for it in the field,
he is obligated for it in the city?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the two possible answers to the question in step 5.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the obligation needs a complete return to begin at all, or whether an obligation that starts in the field carries into the city.

steps.title: The question stays unresolved
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא ends with תיקו: the question is left without an answer.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let it stand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finds no answer, so the question remains open.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sides make sense, and no source settles which one is right. So the question is closed without a decision.

keyTerms.meaning: Let it stand (the question stays unresolved)

steps.whatToRemember: A זקן is exempt from undignified returns, but once he starts handling the animal he must finish (רבה). Whether a return that starts in the field obligates him to continue into the city is left unresolved (תיקו).

phrases.english: Let it stand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the question from steps 5 and 6 without deciding it.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The question of field versus city stays unresolved.

steps.title: רבא's rule: treat another's item like your own
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that whatever a person would do for his own property, he must also do for his friend's property. This applies both to returning lost items and to unloading and loading an animal.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Any case where a person would go and get back his own item, he must also return his friend's item. And any case where he would unload and load his own animal, he must also unload and load his friend's animal.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a practical test for when a respected person may say "this is beneath my dignity" and when he may not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The test is personal: compare how he treats his own things. If he would bother with it for himself, his dignity is not a real excuse, so he must do it for someone else too. The same test covers both השבת אבידה and פריקה וטעינה.

keyTerms.meaning: Returns, or takes back, an item
Unloads a burden from an animal
Loads a burden back onto an animal

steps.whatToRemember: The dignity exemption is measured by you yourself: if you would do it for your own property, you must do it for another person's.
steps.whyThisMatters: This gives a clear practical guideline for the exemption of a זקן ואינו לפי כבודו, in both השבת אבידה and פריקה וטעינה.

phrases.english: Rava said: Any case where with his own he would return it,
phrases.notes: He means: if a dignified person would bother to recover this item if it were his own, he can't use dignity as an excuse.

phrases.english: with his friend's he must also return it.
And any case where with his own he unloads and loads,
with his friend's he must also unload and load.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the תיקו, the גמרא moves to a new general rule that defines the dignity exemption.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person's obligation to return an item or to unload and load is measured by what he would do for his own property.

steps.title: רבי ישמעאל buys the wood instead of lifting it
steps.stepSummary: A man asks רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי to help lift his wood. Instead, רבי ישמעאל pays him its value of half a זוז and declares the wood הפקר.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי was walking on the road. A man met him who was carrying a load of wood. The man put it down and rested, and then said, "Lift it onto me." רבי ישמעאל asked, "How much is it worth?" The man said, "Half a זוז." רבי ישמעאל gave him half a זוז and declared the wood הפקר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story about a great sage who would not lift someone's wood himself. He found another way out instead.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Lifting the wood was not fitting for someone of his stature, and he would not have done it for his own wood either, so by רבא's rule he was exempt. Even so, he went beyond the law: he bought the wood so the man would not lose out, and then gave it up as הפקר.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי הֲוָה קָאָזֵיל בְּאוֹרְחָא,
phrases.english: Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei was walking on the road.
A certain man met him.
He was carrying a load of wood.
He set them down and was resting.
He said to him: Lift it for me.
He said to him: How much are they worth?
He said to him: Half a zuz.
He gave him half a zuz and declared it ownerless.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי הֲוָה קָאָזֵיל בְּאוֹרְחָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A story showing how a sage behaved in a case where lifting was beneath his dignity.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The behavior of רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי, who did not lift the wood himself

steps.title: Ownerless for everyone except you
steps.stepSummary: The man takes the wood back and asks again. רבי ישמעאל pays again and declares it הפקר again. When he sees the man wants to take it once more, he says the wood is הפקר for everyone except him.
steps.simpleTranslation: The man took possession of the wood again. רבי ישמעאל again gave him half a זוז and declared it הפקר. He saw that the man wanted to take it yet again, so he said to him: "I made it ownerless for the whole world, but I did not make it ownerless for you."
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends with רבי ישמעאל making a limited הפקר that leaves out this one man, so the man can't keep taking the wood back.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each time the man took the wood back, he became the owner again and could ask for help again. To end the cycle, רבי ישמעאל made the wood ownerless for everyone else but not for this man. This unusual kind of הפקר is what the גמרא is about to question.

keyTerms.meaning: Again, went back and did it again
For the whole world, for everyone

phrases.english: He then took possession of them again,

phrases.aramaic: הֲדַר יְהַיב לֵיהּ פַּלְגָא דְזוּזָא וְאַפְקְרֵהּ.
phrases.english: He again gave him half a zuz and declared it ownerless.

phrases.aramaic: חַזְיֵיהּ דַּהֲוָה קָא בָּעֵי לְמֶיהְדַּר לְמִזְכֵּיה בְּהוּ,
phrases.english: He saw that he wanted to take possession of them yet again.
He said to him: I made them ownerless for everyone,
phrases.notes: The letters in square brackets are the corrected wording, making it "I made them ownerless."

phrases.english: but for you I did not make them ownerless.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא אַפְקַרְתִּינְהוּ וְלָךְ לָא אַפְקַרְתִּינְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story and reaches its key line: a הפקר that leaves out one person.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי ישמעאל declared the wood הפקר for everyone except the original owner.

steps.title: Can you make something ownerless for some people but not others?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the story with a משנה: בית הלל hold that הפקר only works if it is open to everyone, rich and poor, like שמיטה. So how could רבי ישמעאל leave out one man?
steps.simpleTranslation: But does something become הפקר in a case like this? We learned in a משנה: בית שמאי say that something made ownerless only for poor people is הפקר. בית הלל say it is not הפקר until it is ownerless for poor and rich alike, like produce in the שמיטה year.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions whether רבי ישמעאל's limited הפקר works at all. The next step answers this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We follow בית הלל, who hold that הפקר must be open to everyone, with no one left out. רבי ישמעאל left out the original owner, so by בית הלל his הפקר should not count. The challenge is aimed at the legal validity of his statement, not at the story itself.

keyTerms.meaning: Ownerless property that anyone may take
But didn't we learn in a משנה (introduces a challenge)
The seventh year, when produce is open to everyone

steps.confusionAlert: בית הלל are not saying the poor may not take הפקר. They mean that if you exclude anyone, even only the rich, it is not real הפקר at all.
steps.whyThisMatters: It sets up a basic rule of הפקר: it must be open to everyone, so a selective הפקר is a problem.

phrases.aramaic: וּמִי הָוֵי הֶפְקֵר כִּי הַאי גַוְונָא?
phrases.english: But is it ownerless in a case like this?
But didn't we learn: Beit Shammai say:
phrases.notes: This is a משנה in פאה 6:1.

phrases.english: Ownerless for the poor is ownerless.
And Beit Hillel say:
It is not ownerless until it is ownerless
for the poor and for the rich, like the Sabbatical Year.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִי הָוֵי הֶפְקֵר כִּי הַאי גַוְונָא? וְהָתְנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the legal validity of the selective הפקר in step 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי ישמעאל's declaration that the wood is הפקר for everyone except the original owner
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: בית הלל, whom we follow, require הפקר to be open to everyone. A הפקר that leaves out even one person should not work.

steps.title: The wood was ownerless for everyone; he only asked the man not to take it
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא retells the story: רבי ישמעאל made the wood הפקר for everyone, and only used words to stop the man from taking it back.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי made the wood ownerless for everyone. He just told the man not to take it again.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from Step 11 by explaining the story differently.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 11 asked how a הפקר could leave out one person, since בית הלל say הפקר must be open to all. The answer: he did not leave anyone out legally. The הפקר was complete, and 'except for you' was only a request, not a legal limit.

keyTerms.meaning: He declared them ownerless (made them הפקר)
With mere words, just a statement
He stopped him, held him back

phrases.english: Rather, Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei
declared them ownerless for everyone,
and it was only with a mere statement that he held him back.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי לְכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא אַפְקְרִינְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 11
steps.terutzHavaAmina: He made a הפקר that left out one man, which goes against בית הלל.
steps.terutzMaskana: The הפקר was for everyone. 'Except for you' was only a verbal request.

steps.title: Why get involved if an elder is exempt?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רבי ישמעאל needed to buy the wood at all. As an elder for whom carrying wood is beneath his dignity, he was exempt anyway.
steps.simpleTranslation: But רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי was an elder, and this work was beneath his dignity!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a new difficulty with the story: he had no obligation to help in the first place.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule is that a זקן who would not do such work for himself because of his dignity is exempt from helping. So why did he pay money and make the wood הפקר to get out of a duty he never had?

keyTerms.meaning: But isn't it so that…? (opens a challenge)
An elder for whom the task does not fit his dignity, who is therefore exempt

steps.confusionAlert: This is a new question. It is not about the הפקר problem from Step 11. It asks why he did anything at all.

phrases.english: But wasn't Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei
an elder, and it was not fitting for his dignity!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי זָקֵן וְאֵינָהּ לְפִי כְבוֹדוֹ הֲוָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After defending the הפקר, the גמרא challenges why he acted at all
steps.kashyaTarget: The story of רבי ישמעאל paying for the wood
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: He was exempt as a זקן ואינה לפי כבודו, so there was no reason to pay to free himself.

steps.title: He went beyond the letter of the law
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רבי ישמעאל acted לפנים משורת הדין, doing more than the law required.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי acted beyond the letter of the law.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers Step 13: he knew he was exempt but chose to go further.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The law did not require him to help. He wanted the man to be helped anyway, so he paid for the wood. This was extra goodness, not an obligation.

keyTerms.meaning: Beyond the letter of the law, doing more than required

phrases.english: Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei
acted beyond the letter of the law.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי לִפְנִים מִשּׁוּרַת הַדִּין הוּא דַּעֲבַד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 13
steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing the act was voluntary, beyond what the law requires
steps.terutzHavaAmina: He acted because he was obligated, which makes no sense for an exempt elder.
steps.terutzMaskana: He knew he was exempt and chose to act לפנים משורת הדין.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the idea that going beyond the law is itself something the תורה asks of us.

steps.title: A פסוק that teaches going beyond the law
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף's ברייתא reads each phrase of a פסוק as a different duty, ending with acting לפנים משורת הדין.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רב יוסף taught: 'And you shall make known to them' means their livelihood. 'The path' means acts of kindness. 'They shall walk' means visiting the sick. 'In it' means burial. 'And the action' means the law. 'That they must do' means beyond the letter of the law.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a source showing that going beyond the law is a real value the תורה teaches.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא splits the פסוק into six parts. It separates 'the action' (the strict law) from 'that they must do' (going further). So לפנים משורת הדין is its own instruction, which supports how רבי ישמעאל acted.

phrases.english: As Rav Yosef taught:
"And you shall make known to them": this is their livelihood,
phrases.notes: Literally 'the house of their life.' It means teaching them a way to earn a living.

phrases.english: "the path": this is acts of kindness,
"that they shall walk": this is visiting the sick,
"in it": this is burial,
"and the action": this is the law,
"that they must do": this is beyond the letter of the law.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a source for the idea in Step 14
steps.raayaObject: That acting לפנים משורת הדין is a value the תורה teaches
steps.raayaSupportSource: ברייתא of רב יוסף on שמות 18:20

steps.title: Isn't visiting the sick just an act of kindness?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the ברייתא lists ביקור חולים separately, since it is already part of גמילות חסדים.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: 'that they shall walk' means visiting the sick. But that is the same as acts of kindness!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא looks closely at the ברייתא and points out what seems like a repeat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'The path' already covers acts of kindness, and visiting the sick is one kind of kindness. So why does the פסוק need a separate phrase for it?

keyTerms.meaning: The Master said (quotes the source being discussed)

phrases.english: The Master said:
"that they shall walk": this is visiting the sick.
But that is the same as acts of kindness!

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר מָר אֲשֶׁר יֵלְכוּ זֶה בִּיקּוּר חוֹלִים הַיְינוּ גְּמִילוּת חֲסָדִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Analyzes a detail of the ברייתא in Step 15
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's separate reading of 'אשר ילכו'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: ביקור חולים is already included in גמילות חסדים, so a separate phrase seems unnecessary.

steps.title: You must visit even a sick person your own age
steps.stepSummary: The extra phrase teaches that you must visit a בן גילו, someone your own age, even though the visitor takes on one sixtieth of the illness.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is needed only for someone his own age. As the Master said: someone his own age takes away one sixtieth of his illness. Even so, he must go to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers Step 16: the separate phrase teaches a case we might have thought is exempt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Visiting a sick person your own age has a cost: you take on a little of the illness. You might think this frees you from the duty. The פסוק teaches that you must still go.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed only for… (points to a special case)

steps.whatToRemember: רבי ישמעאל's הפקר was open to everyone. He was exempt as an elder but acted לפנים משורת הדין, a value the תורה itself teaches. Visiting the sick is a separate duty, even for a sick person your own age.

phrases.english: It is needed only for someone his own age,
as the Master said:

phrases.aramaic: בֶּן גִּילוֹ נוֹטֵל אֶחָד מִשִּׁשִּׁים בְּחׇלְיוֹ,
phrases.english: someone his own age takes away one sixtieth of his illness,
and even so
he is required to go to him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 16
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the phrase to a special case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: ביקור חולים is just general kindness, and someone his own age might be exempt because of the cost to himself.
steps.terutzMaskana: The separate phrase teaches that one must visit even a בן גילו, despite taking on one sixtieth of the illness.

steps.title: Why is burial listed separately?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא reads the word בָּהּ as referring to קבורה, and the גמרא asks why. Burial is already included in גמילות חסדים.
steps.simpleTranslation: "Wherein" means burial. But burial is already part of acts of kindness!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next phrase of the ברייתא, which says the word בָּהּ refers to burial. It then challenges this, because burial is already part of גמילות חסדים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same kind of question the גמרא asked about ביקור חולים in step 16. If every phrase of the פסוק teaches a separate duty, then listing burial apart from acts of kindness looks like a repeat. So the extra listing must teach something new.

keyTerms.meaning: "In it" or "wherein," a word from the פסוק

phrases.english: "Wherein" – that is burial.
phrases.notes: This word comes from the same פסוק the ברייתא is reading, שמות 18:20.

phrases.english: That is the same as acts of kindness!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the same kind of challenge as step 16, now aimed at the next phrase of the ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's separate listing of burial
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Burial is already a kind of גמילות חסדים, so a separate phrase for it seems unnecessary.

steps.title: Burial applies even to an elder
steps.stepSummary: The separate phrase teaches that even a זקן, for whom burying the dead is beneath his dignity, must still take part in a burial.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is needed only for an elder, when burying is not fitting for his honor.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that burial is listed on its own to teach a special case: an elder for whom this work is beneath his dignity.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the case of a lost item, a זקן is excused when the work is beneath his dignity. The extra phrase teaches that burial is different. Even such an elder must still help bury the dead.
steps.confusionAlert: This is the opposite of the lost-item rule. With an אבידה, an elder is excused when the work is beneath him. With burial, he is not excused.

phrases.english: It is needed only for an elder
and it is not in keeping with his dignity.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 18.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the phrase to a special case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A זקן for whom burying the dead is beneath his dignity might have been exempt, as he is with a lost item.
steps.terutzMaskana: The phrase teaches that a זקן must help with burial even when it is beneath his dignity.

steps.title: ירושלים was destroyed for sticking to strict law
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא's last phrase teaches acting לפנים משורת הדין. רבי יוחנן shows how serious this is: ירושלים was destroyed because people judged by דין תורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: "That they must do" means going beyond the letter of the law. As רבי יוחנן said: ירושלים was destroyed only because they judged in it by דין תורה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reaches the last phrase of the ברייתא, which is about acting beyond the letter of the law. It brings רבי יוחנן's statement to show how important this is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן's statement shows that going beyond the law is a real duty. Failing to do it was serious enough to bring about the destruction. But his wording is surprising, and the next step questions it.

keyTerms.meaning: "That they must do," the last words of the פסוק

phrases.english: "That they must do"
that is beyond the letter of the law.
As Rabbi Yochanan said:
Jerusalem was destroyed only

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא עַל שֶׁדָּנוּ בָּהּ דִּין תּוֹרָה.
phrases.english: because they judged in it by Torah law.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the last phrase of the ברייתא and supports it with רבי יוחנן's statement.
steps.raayaObject: That going לפנים משורת הדין is a real and serious duty
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי יוחנן's statement about the destruction of ירושלים

steps.title: Should they have judged randomly instead?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי יוחנן's wording. Judging by דין תורה is exactly what judges should do, so the other choice would be judging arbitrarily.
steps.simpleTranslation: But what else should they have done, judged with random rulings?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the wording of רבי יוחנן's statement. Judging by Torah law cannot be a sin.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Read plainly, רבי יוחנן seems to blame people for following the Torah. The only other choice would be baseless rulings, and that is clearly worse. So his words cannot mean what they seem to say.

phrases.english: Rather, should they have judged with arbitrary rulings?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the wording of רבי יוחנן's statement in step 20.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's claim that judging by דין תורה caused the destruction
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Judging by Torah law is required, and the only other choice is arbitrary judgment, which is worse.

steps.title: They held to strict law and never went beyond it
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rereads רבי יוחנן's words. The sin was that people insisted on strict דין תורה every time and never acted לפנים משורת הדין.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, say: they based their rulings only on strict דין תורה and did not go beyond the letter of the law.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains what רבי יוחנן really meant. The problem was not judging by Torah law. The problem was never going any further than that.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Using strict law is fine. Insisting on it in every case, and never giving in or showing kindness, is what was wrong. This ties back to רבי ישמעאל in steps 13–14, who went beyond what the law required of him.

keyTerms.meaning: Say instead, a rereading of the words

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא ends with לפנים משורת הדין. רבי יוחנן teaches that ירושלים was destroyed because people insisted on strict דין תורה and never went beyond it.
steps.whyThisMatters: This closes the side discussion about רבי ישמעאל. It shows that going beyond the letter of the law is a real Torah value, not just something nice to do.

phrases.english: Rather, say:
that they based their rulings on strict Torah law
and did not act beyond the letter of the law.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 21 by rereading רבי יוחנן's words.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי יוחנן seems to blame people for judging by Torah law.
steps.terutzMaskana: The sin was holding only to strict law and never acting לפנים משורת הדין.

steps.title: New משנה: what counts as a lost item
steps.stepSummary: The משנה defines an אבידה. Animals grazing calmly on the road are not lost. A donkey with its gear turned over, or a cow running through vineyards, is lost.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: What counts as lost property? A donkey or cow grazing on the road is not lost. A donkey with its gear overturned, or a cow running among the vineyards, is lost.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It explains when an animal you find counts as lost, which means you must return it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Calm grazing suggests the owner knows where the animal is, so there is nothing to return. Signs of trouble, like overturned gear or running through vineyards, show the animal has really strayed.

phrases.english: Mishnah:
What counts as a lost item?
If he found a donkey or a cow
grazing on the road –
this is not a lost item.
A donkey with its gear turned over,
a cow running among the vineyards –
this is a lost item.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה after the previous discussion ends.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An animal counts as an אבידה only when there are signs it has strayed, not when it is grazing calmly.

steps.title: Return it even if it runs away again and again
steps.stepSummary: If the animal runs away after being returned, the finder must return it again, even four or five times, based on the doubled wording השב תשיבם.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he returned it and it ran away, again and again, even four or five times, he must return it, as it says: "You shall surely return them."
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה teaches that the duty to return a lost animal does not end after one try.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You might think one return is enough to fulfill the מצוה. The משנה learns from the doubled verb in the פסוק that the duty starts again every time the animal runs off.

phrases.english: He returned it and it ran away,
he returned it and it ran away,
even four or five times –
he is obligated to return it,
as it says: "You shall surely return them."
phrases.notes: דברים 22:1. The verb "return" appears twice, and that doubling is the source for returning it again and again.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second rule to the משנה about returning a lost animal.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The finder must keep returning the animal each time it runs away.

steps.title: Paying the finder for lost work time
steps.stepSummary: If returning the item cost the finder a סלע of work, he cannot demand the full סלע. He gets paid like a worker, which is less.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he missed work worth a סלע, he should not say: give me a סלע. Instead, the owner pays him a wage like a worker.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה explains what the finder gets paid when returning the item takes him away from his job.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The finder is paid for his time, but not his full lost earnings. The payment is a worker's wage, which is a smaller amount.

phrases.english: If he was idle from work worth a sela,

phrases.aramaic: לֹא יֹאמַר לוֹ: תֵּן לִי סֶלַע,
phrases.english: he should not say to him: Give me a sela,
rather, he gives him his wage like a worker.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the duty to return the item to how the finder is paid.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The finder receives a worker's wage, not his full lost earnings.

steps.title: Making a condition before a court
steps.stepSummary: If a בית דין is present, the finder can set a condition in front of it to receive full pay. If there is no court, his own money comes first.
steps.simpleTranslation: If there is a court there, he makes a condition before the court. If there is no court, before whom can he make it? His own money comes first.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives the finder a way to protect his full earnings and ends this section of the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a בית דין present, the finder can set a condition to receive full pay for his time. With no court to set a condition before, he does not have to suffer the loss, because his own money takes priority.

keyTerms.meaning: A court, which can be three people

steps.whatToRemember: The finder is normally paid only a worker's wage. He can set a condition before a בית דין to receive full pay. With no court present, his own money comes first.

phrases.english: If there is a court there –
he makes a condition before the court,
if there is no court there –
before whom can he make a condition?
His own comes first.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a way for the finder to receive full pay beyond the worker's wage from step 25.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: With a court present, he may set a condition for full pay. Without one, his own money takes priority.

steps.title: Isn't everything else in the chapter also lost property?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא questions the משנה's wording 'which is an אבידה,' since the whole chapter already deals with lost items.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: Does that mean all the other cases we discussed are not lost items?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pokes at the משנה's wording. If the משנה asks 'what is a lost item?', does that mean all the earlier cases in the chapter were not lost items?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה's question sounds like it is defining the basic idea of אבידה from scratch. But the whole chapter has already been ruling on lost objects. So the wording seems to ignore everything that came before.

keyTerms.meaning: Is that to say...? (a challenge to a reading)

phrases.english: GEMARA: Is that to say that all those cases that we stated
are not lost property?

steps.triggerLanguage: אַטּוּ כֹּל הָנֵי דְּאָמְרִינַן, לָאו אֲבֵידָה הָווּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the opening wording of the משנה summarized in step 23.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's question 'אי זו היא אבידה'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The wording suggests that only these cases are real lost items. That conflicts with the many lost-item cases earlier in the chapter.

steps.title: The משנה means: which lost item must you return?
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה rereads the משנה as asking which lost item creates a duty to return it, then repeats the examples with that wording.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: This is what the משנה means: What is the rule for a lost item that a person must return? If he found a donkey or a cow grazing on the road, it is not lost and he does not have to return it. A donkey with its gear turned over, or a cow running through the vineyards, is lost, and he must return it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה answers the question by adding a few words to the משנה. It is asking which lost items you are obligated to deal with.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה is not defining 'lost' in general. It is setting the rule for when the finder has a duty to act. So the earlier cases stay lost items, and this משנה only marks out which animals trigger the obligation.

keyTerms.meaning: this is what it means (a rereading of a source)
obligated to deal with it (return it)

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said: This is what it is saying:
What is the principle of a lost item
that one is obligated to return?
If he found a donkey or a cow grazing on the road,

phrases.aramaic: אֵין זוֹ אֲבֵידָה וְלָא מִיחַיַּיב בַּהּ.
phrases.english: that is not a lost item, and he is not obligated to return it.
A donkey with its gear turned over,
or a cow running through the vineyards,
that is a lost item, and he is obligated to return it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 27.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה is defining what 'lost' means at all, which would contradict the rest of the chapter.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה defines which lost items obligate the finder to return them.

steps.title: Is a grazing animal never considered lost?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether an animal grazing on the road stays 'not lost' no matter how long it is left there.
steps.simpleTranslation: And is that so forever?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks about the first case: a donkey or cow grazing on the road. Does it never count as lost, no matter how long it stays there?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה gave no time limit. Common sense says an animal left alone long enough must be lost, so the גמרא asks for the boundary.

keyTerms.meaning: and forever? (asking whether a rule has no limit)

phrases.english: And forever?!
phrases.notes: He is asking about the animals grazing on the road. Are they never treated as lost, even after a long time?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Raises a time-limit question about the grazing case in step 28.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How long a grazing animal can be left before it counts as lost.

steps.title: רב: Up to three days
steps.stepSummary: רב rules that a grazing animal is not considered lost only for three days.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: Up to three days.
steps.whatsHappening: רב gives a time limit. For three days the grazing animal is not treated as lost. After that it is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This adds a time limit to the משנה's rule. The fact that the animal is calm and grazing protects it from being called lost only for a while.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
Until three days.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב: עַד שְׁלֹשָׁה יָמִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 29.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A grazing animal is not considered lost for up to three days; after that it is.

steps.title: Three days makes no sense: night or day?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא attacks the three-day rule. At night even one hour should make it lost, and by day even many days should not.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If it is at night, even one hour is enough. If it is during the day, even many days would not make it lost!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב's number by asking when the animal was seen grazing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: People do not leave animals out alone at night, so a night sighting means it is lost right away. Animals do graze alone during the day, so a daytime sighting would never mean lost. Either way, the number 'three days' seems meaningless.

keyTerms.meaning: what is the case? how does it look?

phrases.english: What are the circumstances?
If it was found at night,
then even one hour is also enough to make it lost,
If it was found during the day,
even much longer would also not make it lost!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב's three-day rule from step 30.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Night grazing shows the animal is lost right away. Day grazing never shows it. So a fixed three-day limit seems to fit no case.

steps.title: The case: seen out at dawn and at dusk
steps.stepSummary: The three days apply to an animal seen grazing very early and at nightfall. For three days we assume it just happened to go out early or late. After that it is surely lost.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed where he saw it very early in the morning and in the dark of evening. For three days we say: it just happened to go out then. After more than that, it is surely a lost item.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by finding an in-between case where the three-day count makes sense.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Early morning and dusk are borderline times. An owner might send an animal out a bit early or bring it in a bit late. So for three days we give the benefit of the doubt. If it keeps happening after that, it is no longer chance, and the animal is treated as lost.

keyTerms.meaning: it is only needed for (this case)

steps.whatToRemember: An animal grazing calmly is not lost. But if it is seen out at the edges of the day, very early and at dusk, for more than three days, it is treated as an אבידה.

phrases.english: No, it is necessary
where he saw it in the early morning and in the dark of evening.
For three days we say:
it just happened that it went out then,
more than that, it is certainly a lost item.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא צְרִיכָא, דַּהֲוָה חָזֵי לַהּ בְּקַדְמְתָא וּבַחֲשֶׁכְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 31 by limiting רב's rule to a specific case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The three-day rule applies only to plain night or plain day cases, where it makes no sense.
steps.terutzMaskana: It applies to an animal seen at dawn and dusk. Three days can be chance; more than that means it is lost.

steps.title: A ברייתא supports this: a cloak and an ax
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins quoting a ברייתא that teaches the same idea, starting with someone who found a cloak and an ax.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was also taught this way in a ברייתא: If he found a cloak and an ax...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up support for רב's rule from a ברייתא. Only the opening words appear here, and the ברייתא continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'תניא נמי הכי' tells us a teaching of the תנאים agrees with what was just said. The full proof depends on the rest of the ברייתא, which follows next.

keyTerms.meaning: it was also taught this way (support from a ברייתא)

phrases.english: This is also taught in a baraita:
If one found a cloak or an ax
phrases.notes: This is just the opening of the ברייתא; it continues on the next amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings support from a ברייתא for the three-day rule just explained in step 32.
steps.raayaObject: רב's three-day rule as explained by the גמרא
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about finding a cloak and an ax, which continues on the next amud
